narrative:
The model predicts you have a 40% chance of failing your final year, which is high enough that the school requires you to take remedial courses to strengthen your chances of passing.

The prediction is driven mainly by three aspects of your background. By far the strongest factor is that you have already failed two classes in the past. Among students who passed, the average number of previous failures is zero, so this history strongly pushes the model toward expecting you to fail again. 

Two other features pulled the prediction in the opposite direction. Your family size of three or fewer members is less common among successful students (only 34.5% of passers come from families this small), and this actually works slightly in your favor. Similarly, not having attended nursery school is relatively uncommon among those who passed (only 20.7% of them skipped it), and this also gives a small positive nudge toward passing.

Even with these helpful factors, your past academic failures outweigh them, leading to the decision that extra support is needed. To improve, focus on breaking the pattern of failure by creating a consistent study routine, seeking help early when you struggle with material, and using the remedial courses to fill any gaps from previous years. Small, steady changes now can meaningfully raise your odds of success.
